content.title: How wrong, as one number
content.text: Three pictures, and for each the score the network gave the right digit: 99.75% for the 3, 99.97% for the 8, 0.24% for the 7 it read as a 9. The loss turns that score into a cost: −log of the score. A score of 100% costs nothing, 50% costs 0.69, 10% costs 2.30, and the 7 costs 6.03. The exact rule matters less than its shape: every halving of the score adds the same 0.69, so being confidently wrong costs far more than being unsure. How wrong, as one number per picture.

content.title: One number for all of them
content.text: Average that cost over the 3,823 pictures the network learns from, and the whole network has one number: 0.0416. Before training, with its random start, the same number was 2.29: the right digit got about 10% on average, a guess. Training is nothing but pushing this one number down. It is the score of the knobs, all 2,778 of them at once, and every pill from here on serves it.

content.title: One knob, one picture
content.text: Back to the knob of pill 04, the wire from hidden neuron 6 to the score for 7, at 1.42. Turn it from −6 to 6 and record the loss of the 7 alone. Left, the 7’s score rises and its cost falls, all the way down to 0.39 at −6. Right, the cost climbs past 10. No bottom in sight: if this picture were the whole world, the knob would go left and keep going.

content.title: One knob, every picture
content.text: Now the same knob, the same turn, but the loss averaged over all 3,823 pictures. This curve is a bowl. Steep on the left, exactly where the 7 wanted to go, because there it breaks hundreds of other pictures. Its bottom is at 2.27, a little to the right of where the knob stands. One picture pulls one way, the other 3,822 pull the other, and the average is the referee. That is why this 7 stays wrong: fixing it alone would cost the crowd more than it gains.

content.title: The bottom of the bowl
content.text: Which way, and how far, now has an answer for this knob: downhill, to the bottom. From 1.42 to 2.27 the loss drops from 0.0416 to 0.0412, a tiny gain, because training already left this knob near its bottom. And the bottom is not fixed: it moves whenever any other knob moves. So training is never one jump. It is a small turn, a new measurement, another small turn.

content.title: Two knobs: a bowl to look at
content.text: Add a second knob, a wire into the score for 9, and the loss over both is a surface: lopsided, but a bowl, with one lowest point. The ball is where the network stands, at (1.42, −1.07); the bottom is at (2.40, −1.20), a short roll away. With 2,778 knobs the bowl has 2,778 directions and nobody can draw it or look for its bottom. But at every point it still has a downhill, and that downhill can be read from the numbers alone. Reading it is the slope, the next pill.
